sections.text: Introduction

The requirements of insulating oil used in circuit breakers, as
distinguished from insulating oil used in transformers, are uniquely different.
Modern oil circuit breakers require low viscosity and low pour-point oil since a
large percentage of them are used outdoors and, in many cases, at low
temperatures. All circuit breakers are free breathing (open to atmosphere
through a breathing device). Which does not prevent the admittance of humid air
to the device. In older oil circuit breakers the use of higher viscosity oil is
deemed necessary. The resultant effects of oil mixing and the addition of
inhibitors upon thermal characteristics must be considered.

Recondition circuit breaker oil is much the same manner as
insulating oil; the problem is somewhat different. Whereas sludging may be the
principal problem in a transformer. In a circuit breaker the
chief function of the insulating oil is to quench the arc, so thermal cracking
occurs and minute particles of carbon are formed. These particles, coupled with
moisture, can lower the dielectric breakdown voltage of the oil.
Information
Testing

Testing methods for circuit breaker oils are the same as those
used for insulating oils. Samples are taken in the same manner as for insulating
oil, at specified intervals, varying from a few months to annually. Some of the
established ASTM tests applicable to mineral insulating oils are more
significant to transformers than to circuit breakers, since a circuit breaker is
essentially a free-breathing device that operates at ambient temperature.
New Oil Properties-As Refined

New mineral insulating oils received from the refinery must
confirm to certain qualifying functional requirements listed in ASTM D3187-88
[27].
Test Limits: Shipments of New Mineral Insulating Oil

When mineral insulating oil meeting the qualifications of ASTM
D3487-88 [27] is received in the field for installation in circuit breakers, it
should be checked for certain key values that may be affected by shipment and 
storage. These values are shown in Table 1. Some additional
tests outlined in ASTM D3487-88 [27]; must be performed, however, as a minimum, the tests listed in
Table 1 should be performed.

Viscosity [12 cSt (12 x 10-6 m2/s) maximum
at 40оC] and pour point (- 40оC,
maximum) should be checked in cold climates to ensure that the oil does not
interfere with the free operation of the equipment.
New Oil Properties-Oil Shipped in new equipment

Oil circuit breakers are normally shipped from the factory
 without oil in the tank(s). New oil is processed on-site and the equipment is
 filled with oil. In cases such as these, refer to table 2
New Oil Properties-Prior to Energizing

When mineral-insulating oil is received in bulk shipping
containers, it is processed according to the instructions of the manufacturer
and then introduced into the equipment. Table 2 gives test limits for mineral
circuit breaker insulating oil after being processed, placed in equipment, and
allowing for standing times before energizing.
Service Aged Oil Properties

Suggested limits for continued use of service-aged circuit
breaker oils are shown in Table 3.
Reconditioning

The chief problem in circuit breaker oil maintenance is to keep
the fluid free of water, arc decomposition products, and other contaminants. If
visual examination shows the presence of these materials and the dielectric
strength of the oil drops below an acceptable value, the oil can be
reconditioned, provided it is free of chemical contaminants. The accepted means
of reconditioning is by using blotter papers or paper cartridge filters. This
subject is discussed in detail in IEEE Std 637-1985 [30].
Directives

New 
 mineral insulating oil must be analyzed before charged into equipment or 
 before energizing the transformer to insure that it is agreed with the 
 recommendations in this guide. If the product standards given by the 
 manufacturer differ from recommendations in this guide the manufactures 
 instructions are to be given preference.
